resources.string: Install the firmware, install the firmware update package, and add your games on the Games screen. They will appear here automatically.
EmuCoreV is a PS Vita emulator for Android built on Vita3K.
Play your PS Vita games on Android with the Vita3K core.
Your installed games are collected in one library.
Browse covers, screenshots, videos, and game details in one place.
Install the base firmware and firmware update package before launching games.
Install the main PS Vita firmware package before launching any game.
Install the second firmware package so the emulator has the full required system files.
Choose the folder where your Vita package files are stored.
Android is only exposing one app storage location right now. You can also choose a custom folder if it is available for emulator files.
Choose a packages folder to finish setup.

Firmware files are downloaded directly from Sony’s official update servers. EmuCoreV does not host, mirror, modify, or redistribute firmware from its own resources; it only opens the official public download links and installs the package you choose.
Install games on the Games screen, then refresh the library.

Tap the info icon for a short explanation. Long press a setting title to restore its default value.
Choose what feeds the emulated Vita camera. Solid color and static image act as placeholders; \"Real camera\" uses the device camera when granted.
Show the introductory welcome screen on launch until you dismiss it.

File format used when the emulator captures an in-game screenshot.
Fixes graphical issues for games using the OpenGL renderer. Turn this on if you experience flickering graphics, black screens, or crashes during gameplay. Recommended for most modern Android devices.
Gamepad connected. These settings are applied live while you play.
Connect a physical gamepad to enable these settings.
Emulator data is stored under the selected storage root. Installed games are in `vita/ux0/app`, shader cache and temporary files are in `cache`, and patches are in `patch`.
Allow all files access, then choose the emulator folder again.
Changing storage moves missing emulator data to the selected location. Existing files in the destination are kept.

Back up app preferences and emulator settings to a file, or restore them from a previous backup.
Current app preferences and emulator settings will be replaced with the selected backup.
EmuCoreV is a PS Vita emulator for Android built on the open-source Vita3K project.
Change one option at a time, then test the same game scene so you can see what really improved.

Enables PlayStation TV mode for games that expect it.\n\nUse this when a specific game has compatibility problems, missing system behavior, or unusual loading issues. Leave the default value if games already boot and play correctly, because changing it can introduce new glitches.

Shows FPS and performance stats on top of the game.\n\nUse this when you need performance information while testing a game. Turn it off for normal play, since overlays can distract you and add a small rendering cost.

Sets how much data is shown in the performance overlay.\n\nUse this when you need performance information while testing a game. Turn it off for normal play, since overlays can distract you and add a small rendering cost.

Sets where the performance overlay appears on screen.\n\nUse this when you need performance information while testing a game. Turn it off for normal play, since overlays can distract you and add a small rendering cost.

Fills more of the screen, but may stretch the image.\n\nUse this to improve image clarity, scaling, or visual stability in games that already run well. Reduce it or restore the default if FPS drops, the phone heats up, or graphics become unstable.

Removes the normal frame limit in some games. It can improve speed, but it may break timing.\n\nUse this for testing, skipping slow sections, or working around a game-specific behavior. Avoid it for normal gameplay when timing, physics, cutscenes, or online-style checks need to stay accurate.

Reduces screen tearing, but may lower performance in some games.\n\nUse this to improve image clarity, scaling, or visual stability in games that already run well. Reduce it or restore the default if FPS drops, the phone heats up, or graphics become unstable.

Can fix graphics issues, but usually reduces performance.\n\nUse this to improve image clarity, scaling, or visual stability in games that already run well. Reduce it or restore the default if FPS drops, the phone heats up, or graphics become unstable.

Higher values make the image sharper, but use more GPU power.\n\nUse this to improve image clarity, scaling, or visual stability in games that already run well. Reduce it or restore the default if FPS drops, the phone heats up, or graphics become unstable.

Vulkan is usually the best choice. OpenGL can help on devices with weak Vulkan support.\n\nVulkan is usually the best choice for speed and modern Android drivers. Try OpenGL only when Vulkan fails to boot, shows broken graphics, or your device has poor Vulkan support.

Bilinear smooths the image. Nearest keeps sharper edges.\n\nUse this to improve image clarity, scaling, or visual stability in games that already run well. Reduce it or restore the default if FPS drops, the phone heats up, or graphics become unstable.

Improves texture clarity at angles, but can cost performance.\n\nUse this to improve image clarity, scaling, or visual stability in games that already run well. Reduce it or restore the default if FPS drops, the phone heats up, or graphics become unstable.

Keeps textures in cache to reduce repeated work.\n\nUse this to reduce shader or texture stutter after the first run. Disable it only when a game shows corrupted textures, black screens, or repeatable crashes after caching.

Compiles graphics pipelines in the background to reduce stutter.\n\nUse this to reduce shader or texture stutter after the first run. Disable it only when a game shows corrupted textures, black screens, or repeatable crashes after caching.

Shows when new shaders are compiling.\n\nUse this when you want the emulator interface or in-game system presentation to match your preference. Leave it default if you do not need the extra information or visual change.

Shows a message in the corner during the initial shader caching phase at game startup.\n\nUse this when you want the emulator interface or in-game system presentation to match your preference. Leave it default if you do not need the extra information or visual change.

Can improve speed on some devices, but may cause instability.\n\nUse this when a game is slow, stutters, or your device has enough CPU/GPU headroom to try a faster path. Turn it back off or lower it if you see crashes, audio crackle, overheating, battery drain, or broken timing.

Shows on-screen controls when you are not using a physical controller.\n\nUse this to make touch or controller input feel closer to the way you play. Avoid changing it when controls already feel correct, since extreme values can make aiming, menus, or touch features harder to use.

Shows the touch cursor for games that use front or rear touch input.\n\nUse this to make touch or controller input feel closer to the way you play. Avoid changing it when controls already feel correct, since extreme values can make aiming, menus, or touch features harder to use.

Changes the size of the on-screen controls.\n\nUse this to make touch or controller input feel closer to the way you play. Avoid changing it when controls already feel correct, since extreme values can make aiming, menus, or touch features harder to use.

Changes how transparent the on-screen controls are.\n\nUse this to make touch or controller input feel closer to the way you play. Avoid changing it when controls already feel correct, since extreme values can make aiming, menus, or touch features harder to use.

Turns off motion controls from your device.\n\nUse this to make touch or controller input feel closer to the way you play. Avoid changing it when controls already feel correct, since extreme values can make aiming, menus, or touch features harder to use.

Changes analog stick sensitivity.\n\nUse this to make touch or controller input feel closer to the way you play. Avoid changing it when controls already feel correct, since extreme values can make aiming, menus, or touch features harder to use.
Filters small stick movement near the center to reduce drift. Raise it if the camera or character moves by itself; lower it if aiming feels unresponsive.
Sets how far analog triggers must move before input is sent. Raise it for noisy triggers; lower it for racing or pressure-sensitive controls.
Remaps physical face buttons before they reach the emulator. Use this when your controller layout does not match Vita Cross, Circle, Square, and Triangle placement.
Allows supported games to send vibration to a physical controller or, when fallback is enabled, to the Android device body.
Scales vibration intensity for gamepad rumble and device fallback.
Plays a short pulse using the current vibration strength and routing.
Vibrates the phone or handheld body when a physical controller is missing or does not expose a rumble motor.
Allows supported physical controllers to rumble during gameplay.
Swaps left and right stick axes. Useful for games or controllers with unusual stick routing.
Flips vertical stick movement for camera or aiming controls.

Switches the audio output engine.\n\nUse this when audio is too loud, too quiet, delayed, distorted, or missing in a specific game. Keep defaults if sound is clean, because changing audio paths can add latency or crackle.

Adjusts emulator audio volume.\n\nUse this when audio is too loud, too quiet, delayed, distorted, or missing in a specific game. Keep defaults if sound is clean, because changing audio paths can add latency or crackle.

Keeps Vita NGS audio enabled for normal game audio.\n\nUse this when audio is too loud, too quiet, delayed, distorted, or missing in a specific game. Keep defaults if sound is clean, because changing audio paths can add latency or crackle.

Choose the folder used for local Vita package files.\n\nUse this when you keep Vita packages in a separate folder and want EmuCoreV to find them quickly. Choose a stable folder and avoid temporary download folders that Android or cleaners may delete.

Shows the LiveArea screen before the game starts when needed.\n\nUse this when you want the emulator interface or in-game system presentation to match your preference. Leave it default if you do not need the extra information or visual change.

Shows the Vita system info bar when needed.\n\nUse this when you want the emulator interface or in-game system presentation to match your preference. Leave it default if you do not need the extra information or visual change.
Language used by the EmuCoreV interface.\n\nUse this to match the app or emulated Vita language to the games you play. Leave System/default when you want Android or the game to choose automatically.
Use the same language as Android.

Sets the language reported to the emulated Vita system.\n\nUse this to match the app or emulated Vita language to the games you play. Leave System/default when you want Android or the game to choose automatically.
Choose the language used by the emulated Vita system and games.

Sets the confirm button used by the emulated system.\n\nUse this to make touch or controller input feel closer to the way you play. Avoid changing it when controls already feel correct, since extreme values can make aiming, menus, or touch features harder to use.

Controls how system modules are loaded.\n\nUse this when a specific game has compatibility problems, missing system behavior, or unusual loading issues. Leave the default value if games already boot and play correctly, because changing it can introduce new glitches.

Sets how many worker threads the emulator uses.\n\nUse this when a game is slow, stutters, or your device has enough CPU/GPU headroom to try a faster path. Turn it back off or lower it if you see crashes, audio crackle, overheating, battery drain, or broken timing.

Uses a more aggressive texture cache mode.\n\nUse this to reduce shader or texture stutter after the first run. Disable it only when a game shows corrupted textures, black screens, or repeatable crashes after caching.

Keeps compiled shaders between runs to reduce stutter.\n\nUse this to reduce shader or texture stutter after the first run. Disable it only when a game shows corrupted textures, black screens, or repeatable crashes after caching.

Keeps fullscreen scaling cleaner when possible.\n\nUse this to improve image clarity, scaling, or visual stability in games that already run well. Reduce it or restore the default if FPS drops, the phone heats up, or graphics become unstable.

Loads replacement textures from storage.\n\nUse this for texture packs, modding, or capturing game textures for replacement work. Keep it off for normal play because it can use extra storage, slow loading, or create many files.

Exports game textures to storage.\n\nUse this for texture packs, modding, or capturing game textures for replacement work. Keep it off for normal play because it can use extra storage, slow loading, or create many files.

Exports textures as PNG files.\n\nUse this for texture packs, modding, or capturing game textures for replacement work. Keep it off for normal play because it can use extra storage, slow loading, or create many files.

Adjusts system background music volume.\n\nUse this when audio is too loud, too quiet, delayed, distorted, or missing in a specific game. Keep defaults if sound is clean, because changing audio paths can add latency or crackle.

Shows the touch mode switch during gameplay.\n\nUse this to make touch or controller input feel closer to the way you play. Avoid changing it when controls already feel correct, since extreme values can make aiming, menus, or touch features harder to use.

Runs the game faster than normal. Useful for loading and testing, not regular play.\n\nUse this for testing, skipping slow sections, or working around a game-specific behavior. Avoid it for normal gameplay when timing, physics, cutscenes, or online-style checks need to stay accurate.

Starts games in fullscreen.\n\nUse this when you want the emulator interface or in-game system presentation to match your preference. Leave it default if you do not need the extra information or visual change.

Allows games to use HTTP features when needed.\n\nUse this when a specific game has compatibility problems, missing system behavior, or unusual loading issues. Leave the default value if games already boot and play correctly, because changing it can introduce new glitches.

Reports a signed-in PSN state to games that check it.\n\nUse this when a specific game has compatibility problems, missing system behavior, or unusual loading issues. Leave the default value if games already boot and play correctly, because changing it can introduce new glitches.

Adds an artificial file loading delay for games that need it.\n\nUse this when a specific game has compatibility problems, missing system behavior, or unusual loading issues. Leave the default value if games already boot and play correctly, because changing it can introduce new glitches.

Enables Vulkan validation when the driver supports it.\n\nUse this only when collecting logs or diagnosing a bug. Keep it off for gameplay because debug features can slow the emulator, fill logs, or expose developer-only visual overlays.

Choose between the system Vulkan driver and a custom driver.\n\nUse a custom driver mainly on compatible Adreno devices when the system Vulkan driver has graphical bugs or weak performance. Stay with the system driver on Mali, PowerVR, unknown GPUs, or whenever the custom driver causes crashes.

Choose which installed custom driver to use.\n\nUse a custom driver mainly on compatible Adreno devices when the system Vulkan driver has graphical bugs or weak performance. Stay with the system driver on Mali, PowerVR, unknown GPUs, or whenever the custom driver causes crashes.

EmuCoreV brings PS Vita emulation to Android with a focused mobile interface, local library management, and a Vita3K-based emulation core.
Open the EmuCoreV website for downloads, news, and project links.
View source code, report issues, and follow development on GitHub.
Chat with the community, share feedback, and get project updates.
Help development continue through Patreon membership.
See more Android apps from the developer.
EmuCoreV uses its own Android interface. Only the emulation core is based on Vita3K.
Open the upstream Vita3K project repository.

For major emulator updates, uninstalling the current app before installing the new APK can avoid old files or settings causing problems. Keep backups of important saves before doing that.
Update metadata, release notes, APK size, and the APK download are loaded from the EmuCoreV GitHub releases page.

Android can install multiple EmuCoreV versions only when a release includes a special APK built with a unique package name and app label, such as EmuCoreV (0.1.1). Normal older APKs replace or downgrade the current app.
